overview.title: Computing and plotting one layer activation
overview.main_topic: Running the multi-output activation model on the cat image and plotting a single channel of the first convolution layer's output

summary:
The page continues section 10.1. On the previous page (listing 10.3, p.311) the authors built `activation_model`, a Keras `Model` whose inputs are the original model's input and whose outputs are the outputs of every `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layer. Here they point out what makes that model special: it is the **first multi-output model actually used in practice** in the book (multi-output models were introduced in chapter 7). It has **one input and nine outputs**, one per layer activation.

**Listing 10.4** runs it on the preprocessed cat image: `activations = activation_model.predict(img_tensor)`. The callout explains that the result is a Python list of nine NumPy arrays, one array per layer activation.

The authors then take the first element, the activation of the first convolution layer, and print its shape: `(1, 178, 178, 32)`. That is a batch of one image, with a **178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels**. The 178 comes from applying a 3 × 3 convolution without padding to the 180 × 180 input (180 − 3 + 1 = 178), and the 32 is the number of filters in that `Conv2D` layer, as shown in the model summary on p.309.

**Listing 10.5** plots the sixth channel (index 5) with `plt.matshow(first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5], cmap="viridis")`. **Figure 10.2** shows the result: a dark-blue rendering of the cat in which only some edges light up in bright green/yellow. Most visibly, the right-hand edge of the right ear, a few strokes around the eyes and nose, and a short edge near the chin. On the next page (p.313) the authors interpret this channel as a diagonal edge detector and warn that your own channels may differ because learned filters are not deterministic.

The main point is that each channel of a convolution layer's output is a 2D map of where one learned pattern occurs in the image. That is why section 10.1 says such feature maps should be visualized one channel at a time (p.309).

paragraphs.excerpt: When fed an image input, this model returns the values of the layer activations
paragraphs.what_it_says: Given an image, `activation_model` returns the activation values of the original model's layers as a list. The authors note that this is the first multi-output model you have used in practice since chapter 7. Every model so far had one input and one output, while this one has one input and nine outputs, one per layer activation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In the functional API a model is simply a graph from some input tensors to some output tensors. By choosing as outputs the intermediate symbolic tensors `layer.output` of the trained model, you get a new model that shares all the trained weights but exposes its internal states. There are nine such layers in the cats-vs-dogs convnet: five `Conv2D` and four `MaxPooling2D` layers (p.309–310), hence nine outputs. No new weights are created and nothing is retrained.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the basic tool for inspecting a network: you do not need to change the trained model or write custom forward code. Any intermediate tensor can be turned into an output. The same trick is reused later in the chapter, for example in section 10.3 a model is built that maps the input image to the activations of the last convolutional layer (p.325).
paragraphs.technical_idea: A functional `keras.Model(inputs, outputs=[t1,...,t9])` returns a list from `predict` whose order matches the `outputs` list. Here that is the order in which listing 10.3 appended layers while looping over `model.layers`.

terminology.meaning: The output of a layer (in the book's words, the output of the activation function) for a given input (p.309).
A functional model whose `outputs` argument is a list of several tensors; `predict` then returns a list of arrays.

connections: p.309: the model summary lists the Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers whose outputs are exposed
p.325: section 10.3 again builds a model returning an intermediate (last conv) activation

paragraphs.what_it_says: The first element of the returned list is the activation of the first convolution layer for the cat image, and its printed shape is `(1, 178, 178, 32)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Axis 0 is the batch axis: `img_tensor` holds a single image because `get_img_array` called `np.expand_dims(..., axis=0)` (p.310). Axes 1 and 2 are the spatial height and width. The size is 178, not 180, because the first `Conv2D` uses a 3 × 3 kernel without padding, which shrinks each side by 2. Axis 3 holds the 32 channels, one per filter of that layer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reading this shape correctly is what allows the slicing in listing 10.5. It also confirms that the activation model output matches the `(None, 178, 178, 32)` row of the model summary, with `None` replaced by the actual batch size 1.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Valid convolution output size: $H_{out} = H_{in} - k + 1 = 180 - 3 + 1 = 178$ (stride 1).

terminology.meaning: A rank-3 tensor (height, width, channels) produced by a convolution or pooling layer; each channel is a 2D map of one feature.
The leading dimension indexing independent samples; here of size 1.

connections: p.262: border effects, a 3 × 3 window shrinks a feature map by two tiles along each dimension
p.310: `get_img_array` adds the batch axis with `np.expand_dims`

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors restate the shape in words, a 178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels, and propose plotting the sixth channel of the first layer's activation, which is shown in figure 10.2.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each of the 32 channels is the response of one learned 3 × 3 × 3 filter (followed by ReLU) at every location of the image. Plotting one channel as an image shows where in the cat picture that filter's pattern is present. 'Sixth channel' means index 5 because Python indexing starts at 0.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This follows the principle stated at the start of the section: since channels encode relatively independent features, the right way to visualize a feature map is to plot each channel separately as a 2D image (p.309).

concepts.name: Intermediate activation
concepts.definition: The output of a hidden layer (here a Conv2D or MaxPooling2D layer) for a particular input.
concepts.intuition: It is a snapshot of how the network has re-described the image at that depth.
concepts.technical: For a convnet layer it is a tensor of shape `(batch, height, width, channels)`; for the first layer of this model `(1, 178, 178, 32)`.
concepts.significance: Visualizing intermediate activations is the first of the three interpretation techniques in chapter 10 and shows how an input is decomposed by the learned filters (p.309).
concepts.example: `activations[0]` holds the 32 feature maps of `conv2d_11` for the cat image.
concepts.misconception: An activation is not a filter: the filter is the weight kernel, while the activation is what that kernel produces on a specific image.

concepts.name: Multi-output model
concepts.definition: A functional Keras model built with a list of output tensors, which returns a list of arrays from `predict`.
concepts.intuition: Instead of only reading the final answer, you put probes at several points in the network and read them all at once.
concepts.technical: `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)` where `layer_outputs` contains the symbolic outputs of nine existing layers; the new model shares the trained weights.
concepts.significance: Per the page, this is the first multi-output model used in practice in the book; it is what makes feature-map inspection a one-liner.
concepts.example: `activation_model` has one input and nine outputs.
concepts.misconception: Building it does not copy or retrain anything. It reuses the same layer objects and weights.

concepts.name: Feature map (channel view)
concepts.definition: A rank-3 tensor of spatial positions × channels; each channel is a 2D grid recording how strongly one filter responds at each location.
concepts.intuition: Think of 32 transparent overlays on the image, each highlighting where a particular small pattern occurs.
concepts.technical: Channel $c$ of a Conv2D+ReLU output at position $(i,j)$ is $\operatorname{relu}(\sum_{u,v,d} K_c[u,v,d]\,x[i+u,j+v,d] + b_c)$.
concepts.significance: Because channels are relatively independent, each is plotted separately (p.309).
concepts.example: `first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5]` is a 178 × 178 map shown in figure 10.2.
concepts.misconception: The colors in figure 10.2 are not the image's colors; they are a colormap applied to a single number per pixel.

concepts.name: Valid convolution border effect
concepts.definition: Without padding, a k × k convolution with stride 1 can only be centered on positions where the window fits, so the output loses k − 1 rows and columns.
concepts.intuition: A 3 × 3 stamp cannot be centered on the outermost ring of pixels.
concepts.significance: Explains the 178 × 178 spatial size on this page.
concepts.misconception: The shrinking is not caused by pooling; pooling comes after this layer (89 × 89, p.310).

math.title: Spatial size of the first convolution output

variables.meaning: Kernel size of the Conv2D layer: 3
Output height (and width) with stride 1 and no padding

math.operations: Subtract the kernel size from the input size and add one.
math.purpose: Explain where the 178 in the printed shape comes from.
math.interpretation: Each output position corresponds to one valid placement of the 3 × 3 window.
math.intuition: One pixel is lost on each border, two per dimension.
math.numerical_example: Number of activation values in this layer: $178 \times 178 \times 32 = 1{,}013{,}888$. Plotting channel 5 shows $178^2 = 31{,}684$ of them.

code.title: Using the model to compute layer activations
code.what_it_does: Runs a forward pass of the activation model on the cat image and collects the outputs of all nine Conv2D/MaxPooling2D layers.

line_explanations.explanation: `predict` takes the batch `img_tensor` of shape (1, 180, 180, 3) and, because the model has nine outputs, returns a list of nine NumPy arrays (book callout: 'Returns a list of nine NumPy arrays—one array per layer activation').

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `img_tensor`, shape (1, 180, 180, 3), raw pixel values (the model's own Rescaling layer normalizes them). Output: list of 9 arrays with shapes (1,178,178,32), (1,89,89,32), (1,87,87,64), (1,43,43,64), (1,41,41,128), (1,20,20,128), (1,18,18,256), (1,9,9,256), (1,7,7,512), following the summary on p.309–310.
code.algorithm: Single forward pass; all intermediate tensors requested as outputs are returned rather than discarded.
code.theory_link: Functional-API models are graphs of layers; any node can be an output (chapter 7).

parameters.role: Batch containing the single test cat image (listing 10.1).

pitfalls: Forgetting the batch axis: passing a (180, 180, 3) array instead of (1, 180, 180, 3) would fail.

code.title: Visualizing the sixth channel
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.matshow(first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5], cmap="viridis")
code.what_it_does: Displays the 178 × 178 map of channel index 5 as a color-coded image (figure 10.2).

line_explanations.explanation: `[0, :, :, 5]` selects image 0 of the batch, all rows, all columns, channel 5 (the sixth). `plt.matshow` draws a 2D array as a matrix image with axes labeled by index, and `cmap="viridis"` maps low values to dark blue and high values to yellow.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: rank-4 activation array. Output: a figure like 10.2 with 0–160+ tick labels on both axes.
code.algorithm: Slice a 2D array from a rank-4 tensor and render it with a colormap (auto-scaled to the array's min/max).
code.theory_link: Each channel encodes a relatively independent feature, so it is plotted on its own (p.309).

parameters.role: Channel index; try 0–31 to see the other filters of the first layer.

parameters.name: cmap
parameters.role: Colormap used to turn scalar activations into colors.

pitfalls: Channel indices start at 0, so the 'sixth channel' is index 5.
Because matshow normalizes per image, brightness levels are not comparable across separately plotted channels.
Your channel 5 may look different from figure 10.2, since training is not deterministic (p.313).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: browse the first 8 channels side by side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(16, 2))
for c, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.matshow(first_layer_activation[0, :, :, c], cmap="viridis")
    ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

deeper.title: Why nine outputs? Counting the exposed layers
deeper.body:
Listing 10.3 keeps only layers that are `Conv2D` or `MaxPooling2D`. In the model summary (p.309–310) these are, in order:

1. `conv2d_11` → (178, 178, 32)
2. `max_pooling2d_6` → (89, 89, 32)
3. `conv2d_12` → (87, 87, 64)
4. `max_pooling2d_7` → (43, 43, 64)
5. `conv2d_13` → (41, 41, 128)
6. `max_pooling2d_8` → (20, 20, 128)
7. `conv2d_14` → (18, 18, 256)
8. `max_pooling2d_9` → (9, 9, 256)
9. `conv2d_15` → (7, 7, 512)

The input, Rescaling, GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dropout and Dense layers are skipped. Hence nine outputs. (Shapes taken from the book's summary; the ordered list is an explanatory aid.)

deeper.title: Reading figure 10.2
deeper.body: In figure 10.2, the background and most of the fur are uniformly dark blue, meaning near-zero activation (ReLU clips negative responses to 0). The bright yellow-green strokes run mainly along one orientation: the outer edge of the right ear, parts of the eye outlines and a stroke near the chin. A filter that responds to intensity changes along a particular direction behaves this way, which is why the authors call it a diagonal edge detector on p.313. The faint outline of the whole cat remains visible, showing that early activations still keep most of the picture's information (p.314).

deeper.title: Activations as overlays
deeper.body: Imagine 32 sheets of tracing paper over the photo. Each sheet belongs to one small 'pattern detector' and is shaded wherever its pattern appears. Figure 10.2 is sheet number 6. Section 10.1 continues by laying out all sheets of all nine layers in one grid (figure 10.3).

visualizations.title: Shapes of the nine activations returned by listing 10.4
visualizations.why: The page says the model returns nine arrays and prints the first one's shape (1, 178, 178, 32); this traces how that shape evolves through all nine exposed layers (shapes from the model summary on p.309–310).

visualizations.title: How one channel of a feature map is computed
visualizations.why: Figure 10.2 shows one channel of the first Conv2D output, which responds to diagonal edges according to p.313. Stepping a 3 × 3 diagonal-edge kernel over a small image with a diagonal shows how such a channel lights up only along the matching structure (the kernel is illustrative; the real learned kernel is not printed).

misconceptions.claim: `activation_model` is a new network that had to be trained.
misconceptions.correction: It reuses the trained layers and weights of `model`; it only exposes their outputs.

misconceptions.claim: The 178 × 178 size is due to resizing or pooling.
misconceptions.correction: It is the border effect of a 3 × 3 convolution without padding on a 180 × 180 input; pooling halves it only in the next layer (89 × 89).

misconceptions.claim: Figure 10.2 is a colored version of the photo.
misconceptions.correction: It is one channel of the activation, a single scalar per position rendered with the viridis colormap.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone running this code will see the same channel 5.
misconceptions.correction: Learned filters depend on random initialization and training, so channel contents and order differ between runs (p.313).

takeaways: `activation_model` has one input and nine outputs, so `predict` returns a list of nine NumPy arrays.
The first convolution layer's activation has shape (1, 178, 178, 32): batch, height, width, channels.
178 = 180 − 3 + 1, the border effect of an unpadded 3 × 3 convolution.
`first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5]` extracts the sixth channel as a 178 × 178 2D map.
`plt.matshow` with a colormap turns that map into an image; figure 10.2 shows a filter that highlights certain edges of the cat.

questions.question: Why does `activation_model.predict(img_tensor)` return a list rather than a single array?
options: Because predict always returns lists in Keras
Because the model was built with nine output tensors, one per Conv2D/MaxPooling2D layer
Because the model has nine inputs
questions.answer: Because the model was built with nine output tensors, one per Conv2D/MaxPooling2D layer
questions.explanation: The page states the model has one input and nine outputs, one per layer activation. Single-output models return a single array, so predict does not always return a list. img_tensor has batch size 1, and there is only one input.

questions.question: Interpret each axis of the shape (1, 178, 178, 32).
questions.answer: 1 = batch size (one image), 178 = height, 178 = width, 32 = channels (number of filters in the first Conv2D layer).
questions.explanation: The page calls it a 178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels; the leading 1 is the batch axis added by np.expand_dims in listing 10.1.

questions.question: The input is 180 × 180 and the first layer is a 3 × 3 Conv2D without padding. Derive the output spatial size, and compute how many scalar values the whole first-layer activation contains.
questions.explanation: A valid 3 × 3 convolution loses one pixel on each border (p.262). Multiplying height, width and channels gives the element count.

questions.question: What expression would you pass to `plt.matshow` to view the 20th channel of the first layer's activation?
questions.explanation: Indexing is zero-based, just as the sixth channel is index 5 in listing 10.5; the leading 0 selects the only image in the batch.

questions.question: Why do the authors plot a single channel rather than trying to display the whole (178, 178, 32) activation as one image?
questions.answer: Because each channel encodes a relatively independent feature, so each must be shown as its own 2D image; 32 channels cannot be rendered as one color image meaningfully.
questions.explanation: Section 10.1 (p.309) states that the proper way to visualize feature maps is to plot every channel independently as a 2D image. A normal image has only 3 color channels.

questions.question: What does figure 10.2 primarily show?
options: The learned 3 × 3 weights of the sixth filter
The cat image after rescaling to [0, 1]
Where in the cat image the sixth first-layer filter responds strongly
questions.answer: Where in the cat image the sixth first-layer filter responds strongly
questions.explanation: It plots `first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5]`, a response map. The filter weights themselves are visualized differently in section 10.2. The image is not shown as raw pixels, and class heatmaps are the topic of section 10.3.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, how a model with one input and nine outputs is created from an already trained model, and why it needs no retraining?
questions.answer: Collect `layer.output` for the chosen layers and call `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)`; it reuses the same layers and weights.
questions.explanation: If this is unclear, revisit listing 10.3 on p.311 and the functional API in chapter 7.
